statute_title: Operating a Vehicle Under the Influence of an Intoxicant (OVUII)
offense_class: Petty Misdemeanor (first offense); Misdemeanor (second within 10 years); Class C Felony (third+ within 10 years)
elements: Defendant operated or assumed actual physical control of a vehicle
On a public way, street, road, or highway
While under the influence of alcohol or any drug that impaired the ability to operate safely
OR with BAC of .08 or more
mandatory_minimum: 14 hours community service (first); 240 hours community service or 5 days imprisonment (second); 10 days imprisonment (third)
enhancements: Minor passenger under 15 years of age
Third or subsequent offense within 10 years (Class C felony)
Causing serious bodily injury or death (separate charges under HRS § 291E-61.5)
notes: Hawaii uses the term OVUII rather than DUI/DWI. Implied consent under HRS § 291E-11. Administrative license revocation separate from criminal penalties. Ignition interlock required for repeat offenses.

statute_title: OVUII — First Offense
elements: Defendant operated or assumed actual physical control of a vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol or drugs impairing ability to operate safely
OR BAC of .08 or more
No prior OVUII convictions within 10 years
notes: Substance abuse assessment required. Court may order alcohol or drug treatment program. License revocation is 1 year for first offense.

statute_title: OVUII — Repeat Offense
offense_class: Misdemeanor (second within 10 years); Class C Felony (third+ within 10 years)
elements: Defendant operated or assumed actual physical control of a vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol or drugs
OR BAC of .08 or more
One or more prior OVUII convictions within 10 years
mandatory_minimum: 240 hours community service or 5 days imprisonment (second); 10 days imprisonment (third+)
enhancements: Third offense within 10 years (Class C felony)
notes: Mandatory ignition interlock device. Extended license revocation. Mandatory substance abuse treatment program.

statute_title: OVUII — Drug Impairment
offense_class: Petty Misdemeanor (first); escalates same as alcohol OVUII
penalty_max: 30 days (first); same escalation as alcohol OVUII
elements: Defendant operated or assumed actual physical control of a vehicle
While under the influence of any drug that impaired ability to operate the vehicle safely
Impairment rendered the person incapable of driving safely
mandatory_minimum: Same as alcohol OVUII by offense count
notes: No per se drug limit in Hawaii. Prosecution must prove impairment. Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluations commonly used.

statute_title: Reckless Driving of Vehicle or Riding of Animals
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle or rode an animal on a highway
Recklessly in disregard of the safety of persons or property
notes: Often charged as a lesser included offense in OVUII cases. Highway includes any public road or street in Hawaii.

statute_title: Accidents Involving Death or Serious Bodily Injury — Duty to Stop
offense_class: Class B Felony (death or serious bodily injury); Class C Felony (bodily injury); Misdemeanor (property only, HRS § 291C-13)
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident
Accident resulted in injury or death to any person (or damage to property)
Defendant failed to immediately stop at the scene or render aid
Defendant failed to give information and render assistance as required
enhancements: Accident resulting in death (Class B felony)
Leaving the scene of a fatality (additional penalties)
notes: Driver must provide name, address, registration number, and exhibit driver's license. Must render reasonable assistance to injured persons.

statute_title: Negligent Homicide in the First Degree
elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
By operation of a vehicle in a negligent manner
enhancements: Operating under the influence at time of offense
notes: Hawaii does not have a separate vehicular homicide statute — negligent homicide covers vehicle-related deaths. See also HRS § 707-703 for negligent homicide in second and third degree.

statute_title: Manslaughter — Reckless Causing of Death (Vehicle Context)
offense_class: Class A Felony (reckless manslaughter); Class B Felony (negligent)
elements: Defendant recklessly caused the death of another person
Death occurred in the context of operating a motor vehicle
notes: Manslaughter in Hawaii is recklessly causing the death of another. When a vehicle is involved, this statute applies rather than a separate vehicular manslaughter provision.

statute_title: Driving While License Suspended or Revoked
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle on a public highway
While defendant's license was suspended, revoked, or restricted
Defendant had knowledge of the suspension or revocation
enhancements: Driving while license suspended for OVUII (enhanced penalties)
Prior convictions for driving on suspended
notes: Separate from HRS § 291E-62 (driving after OVUII administrative revocation), which carries additional mandatory minimums.

statute_title: Resisting an Order to Stop a Motor Vehicle in the Second Degree
offense_class: Misdemeanor; Class C Felony (first degree under HRS § 710-1026.8 if risk of death or SBI)
elements: Defendant intentionally failed to obey a direction of a law enforcement officer
Direction was to stop the defendant's motor vehicle
Law enforcement officer was acting under color of official authority
enhancements: Creating a risk of death or serious bodily injury (first degree — Class C felony)
Operating under the influence while fleeing
notes: First degree (HRS § 710-1026.8) applies when fleeing creates substantial risk of death or serious bodily injury.

statute_title: Consuming or Possessing Intoxicating Liquor While Operating Motor Vehicle
elements: Defendant consumed or possessed an open container of intoxicating liquor
While operating a motor vehicle on a public highway
notes: Open container laws in Hawaii are less strict than many mainland states. Passengers may possess open containers in some circumstances.

statute_title: Refusal to Submit to Breath, Blood, or Urine Test
offense_class: Administrative penalty (license revocation); no separate criminal charge for refusal
elements: Defendant was lawfully arrested for OVUII
Defendant was informed of the implied consent law
Defendant refused to submit to a breath, blood, or urine test
notes: Hawaii's implied consent law (HRS § 291E-11) does not impose a separate criminal charge for refusal but imposes administrative license revocation. Refusal can be used as evidence in the underlying OVUII prosecution.

statute_title: Promoting a Dangerous Drug in the Third Degree
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed any dangerous drug in any amount
notes: Dangerous drugs include methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin, and other Schedule I/II substances. Hawaii treats simple possession as a felony. Deferred acceptance of guilty plea available for first offenders.

statute_title: Promoting a Detrimental Drug in the Third Degree
offense_class: Petty Misdemeanor (possession of 3 grams or less); Misdemeanor (possession of 1 oz or less); Class C Felony (over 1 oz under HRS § 712-1247)
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed marijuana
Amount determines the degree of offense
enhancements: Distribution (elevates to first or second degree promoting)
Cultivation of 25+ plants (Class B felony under HRS § 712-1249.5)
notes: Hawaii has a medical marijuana program under HRS Chapter 329. Possession of 3 grams or less was decriminalized (no jail, fine only). Amounts over 1 oz are felony-level under HRS § 712-1247.

statute_title: Promoting a Dangerous Drug in the Third Degree — Cocaine
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed cocaine in any amount
Cocaine is classified as a dangerous drug under HRS § 712-1240
enhancements: Possession of 1/8 ounce or more (second degree — Class B felony under HRS § 712-1242)
notes: Any amount of cocaine possession is a Class C felony. Quantities of 1/8 oz or more elevate to Class B felony (second degree promoting).

statute_title: Promoting a Dangerous Drug in the Third Degree — Methamphetamine
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed methamphetamine in any amount
Methamphetamine is classified as a dangerous drug under HRS § 712-1240
enhancements: Possession of 1/8 ounce or more (second degree — Class B felony under HRS § 712-1242)
Possession of 1 ounce or more (first degree — Class A felony under HRS § 712-1241)
notes: Methamphetamine is a major enforcement priority in Hawaii. First degree promoting (1 oz+) is a Class A felony with up to 20 years imprisonment.

statute_title: Promoting a Dangerous Drug in the Third Degree — Opioids
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed heroin, fentanyl, or other opioids in any amount
Substance is classified as a dangerous drug under HRS § 712-1240
enhancements: Possession of 1/8 ounce or more of heroin (second degree — Class B felony)
notes: Heroin and fentanyl are classified as dangerous drugs. Opioid prescription medications possessed without valid prescription also fall under this statute.

statute_title: Promoting a Harmful Drug in the Third Degree
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed a harmful drug without a valid prescription
Harmful drugs include Schedule III-V controlled substances
enhancements: Distribution (elevates to first or second degree)
notes: Harmful drugs include anabolic steroids, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and other Schedule III-V substances possessed without prescription.

statute_title: Promoting a Dangerous Drug in the First Degree
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed one or more preparations of a dangerous drug
In an aggregate weight of 1 ounce or more containing methamphetamine, heroin, morphine, or cocaine
OR 1 ounce or more of any other dangerous drug
OR possessed one or more preparations of 50 or more capsules or tablets
enhancements: Use of a minor in drug operations
notes: First degree promoting is Hawaii's most serious drug charge. Class A felony carries indeterminate 20-year maximum with minimum set by parole authority.

statute_title: Promoting a Dangerous Drug in the Second Degree
penalty_min: 5 years (indeterminate minimum set by parole authority)
elements: Defendant knowingly distributed any dangerous drug in any amount
OR possessed 1/8 ounce or more of methamphetamine, heroin, morphine, or cocaine
OR possessed 50 or more capsules, tablets, or units of a dangerous drug
notes: Distribution means to sell, transfer, give, deliver, barter, or exchange. Second degree covers both distribution of any amount and possession of threshold quantities.

statute_title: Promoting a Dangerous Drug in the First Degree — Manufacturing
elements: Defendant knowingly manufactured or cultivated a dangerous drug
Drug was a substance classified under HRS § 712-1240
enhancements: Manufacturing near schools or residential areas
Manufacturing methamphetamine in presence of minors
notes: Manufacturing any dangerous drug is treated as first degree promoting regardless of quantity. Methamphetamine lab operations are heavily prosecuted.

statute_title: Prohibited Acts Related to Drug Paraphernalia
elements: Defendant used, or possessed with intent to use, drug paraphernalia

Paraphernalia was used to plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, harvest, manufacture, compound, convert, produce, process, prepare, test, analyze, pack, repack, store, contain, conceal, inject, ingest, inhale, or otherwise introduce into the body a controlled substance
enhancements: Delivery of drug paraphernalia to a minor (Class C felony)
notes: Drug paraphernalia includes items used for ingesting, inhaling, or injecting controlled substances. Delivery to a minor elevates the charge.

statute_title: Prohibited Acts — Fraud in Obtaining Controlled Substances
elements: Defendant obtained or attempted to obtain a controlled substance by fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, or subterfuge
OR used a false name or gave a false address in obtaining or attempting to obtain a controlled substance
enhancements: Multiple prescriptions from different providers (doctor shopping)
notes: Includes doctor shopping, forging prescriptions, and altering prescriptions. Each fraudulent obtaining is a separate offense.

statute_title: Promoting a Dangerous Drug in the Second Degree — Possession with Intent
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed a dangerous drug
In a quantity indicating intent to distribute (1/8 oz+ of meth/cocaine/heroin or 50+ units)
OR evidence of intent to distribute (scales, packaging, large cash)
enhancements: Exceeding first-degree thresholds (1 oz+ — Class A felony)
notes: Hawaii uses quantity thresholds rather than explicit 'possession with intent' language. Threshold quantities create a presumption of distribution intent.

statute_title: Murder in the First Degree
offense_class: Class A Felony (life imprisonment without possibility of parole)
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused the death of another person
With premeditation
OR during the course of specified felonies (felony murder)
OR victim was a witness, law enforcement officer, judge, or prosecutor in an official capacity
OR multiple victims killed
mandatory_minimum: Life imprisonment without possibility of parole
enhancements: Killing of a law enforcement officer or official
notes: Hawaii abolished the death penalty in 1957. First degree murder carries mandatory life without parole. HRS § 706-656 governs the sentence.

statute_title: Murder in the Second Degree
offense_class: Class A Felony (life imprisonment with possibility of parole)
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused the death of another person
Without premeditation or other first-degree aggravating factors
mandatory_minimum: Minimum term set by Hawaii Paroling Authority (typically not less than 10 years)
enhancements: Use of a firearm (mandatory minimum enhanced)
notes: Second degree murder is an intentional killing without the aggravating factors required for first degree. Parole eligibility determined by the Hawaii Paroling Authority.

statute_title: Manslaughter — Reckless
elements: Defendant recklessly caused the death of another person
notes: Hawaii does not distinguish between voluntary and involuntary manslaughter by name. Manslaughter under HRS § 707-702(1) covers reckless killings, which includes heat-of-passion killings that might be voluntary manslaughter in other jurisdictions.

statute_title: Manslaughter — Intentional or Knowing Causing of Death Under Extreme Mental or Emotional Disturbance
offense_class: Class A Felony (HRS § 707-702(1)); Class B Felony (negligent homicide under HRS § 707-702.5)
elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
Through criminal negligence (negligent homicide)
OR recklessly (manslaughter)
notes: Hawaii covers what other states call involuntary manslaughter through both manslaughter (reckless) and negligent homicide (HRS § 707-702.5). Negligent homicide has three degrees.

statute_title: Assault in the Second Degree
elements: Defendant recklessly caused serious or substantial bodily injury to another
OR intentionally or knowingly caused bodily injury to another with a dangerous instrument
OR intentionally or knowingly caused bodily injury to a correctional worker, emergency personnel, or educational worker
enhancements: Use of a dangerous instrument or weapon
Victim is a public official or emergency worker
Assault in the first degree (HRS § 707-710) if serious bodily injury is intentionally caused — Class B felony
notes: Assault in the first degree (HRS § 707-710, Class B felony) applies when the defendant intentionally or knowingly causes serious bodily injury.

statute_title: Assault in the Third Degree
elements: Defendant intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly caused bodily injury to another person
OR negligently caused bodily injury to another with a dangerous instrument
enhancements: Against a sports official (separate offense under HRS § 707-712.6)
notes: Third degree assault is the most commonly charged assault offense in Hawaii. Bodily injury means physical pain, illness, or any impairment of physical condition.

statute_title: Assault in the Third Degree (Hawaii Combines Assault and Battery)
elements: Defendant caused bodily injury to another person
Intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly
notes: Hawaii combines assault and battery into a single offense category. There is no separate battery statute. All offensive touching that causes bodily injury is prosecuted as assault.

statute_title: Assault in the First Degree
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused serious bodily injury to another person
OR intentionally or knowingly caused bodily injury to another with a dangerous instrument creating a substantial risk of death
enhancements: Victim is a first responder, correctional worker, or government official
notes: Serious bodily injury means bodily injury which creates a substantial risk of death or causes serious permanent disfigurement, protracted loss, or impairment of a bodily member or organ.

statute_title: Robbery in the Second Degree
elements: Defendant, in the course of committing a theft from a person
Used force against the person of anyone present with intent to overcome resistance to the theft
OR threatened the imminent use of force
enhancements: Infliction of serious bodily injury (may elevate to first degree)
Armed with a dangerous instrument (first degree)
notes: Robbery is theft from a person by force or threat of force. Second degree is the base offense; first degree applies with aggravating factors.

statute_title: Robbery in the First Degree
elements: Defendant, in the course of committing a theft or non-consensual taking of a motor vehicle
Was armed with a dangerous instrument or simulated firearm
OR inflicted or attempted to inflict serious bodily injury on another
enhancements: Use of a firearm (mandatory minimum under HRS § 706-660.1)
notes: First degree robbery is one of the most serious property offenses. Mandatory minimum of imprisonment may apply when a firearm is used.

statute_title: Kidnapping
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly restrained another person
With intent to hold for ransom, reward, or shield
OR facilitate commission of a felony or flight from a felony
OR inflict bodily injury or terrorize the victim
OR interfere with government or political function
notes: Kidnapping is a Class A felony carrying up to 20 years. Unlawful imprisonment (HRS § 707-721, Class C felony; § 707-722, Misdemeanor) covers lesser restraint offenses.

statute_title: Arson in the First Degree
offense_class: Class A Felony (first degree); Class B Felony (second degree, HRS § 708-8252); Class C Felony (third degree, HRS § 708-8253)
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly set fire to or caused to be burned property
And thereby recklessly placed another person in danger of death or bodily injury (first degree)
OR intentionally or knowingly damaged property of another by fire (second degree)
notes: Hawaii has four degrees of arson. First degree requires reckless endangerment of life. Fourth degree (HRS § 708-8254) is a misdemeanor for reckless burning.

statute_title: Criminal Attempt — Murder
offense_class: Class A Felony (attempt of murder 1st or 2nd degree)
elements: Defendant intentionally engaged in conduct which would constitute murder
OR intentionally engaged in conduct constituting a substantial step toward commission of murder
Defendant had the intent to cause the death of another person
notes: Attempted murder is graded one level below the completed offense under HRS § 705-502, but attempted first or second degree murder remains a Class A felony.

statute_title: Assault in the Second Degree — Dangerous Instrument
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused bodily injury to another person
With a dangerous instrument
enhancements: Serious bodily injury caused (may elevate to first degree assault — Class B felony)
Use of a firearm (mandatory minimum under HRS § 706-660.1)
notes: Dangerous instrument includes any firearm, weapon, or other instrument that in the manner used is capable of producing death or serious bodily injury.

statute_title: Theft
offense_class: Class B Felony (first degree, $20,000+); Class C Felony (second degree, $750+); Misdemeanor (third degree, $250+); Petty Misdemeanor (fourth degree, under $250)
elements: Defendant obtained or exerted unauthorized control over the property of another
With intent to deprive the owner of the property
enhancements: Theft of a firearm (Class B felony regardless of value)
notes: Hawaii consolidates all theft offenses under HRS § 708-830. Degree based on value: 1st ($20,000+), 2nd ($750+), 3rd ($250+), 4th (under $250).

statute_title: Theft in the First Degree
elements: Defendant obtained or exerted unauthorized control over property of another
Value exceeds $20,000
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: First degree theft applies when the value of property exceeds $20,000 or the property is a firearm.

statute_title: Theft in the Fourth Degree
elements: Defendant obtained or exerted unauthorized control over property of another
Value under $250
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Fourth degree theft is the lowest theft offense. Community service often imposed in lieu of jail for first offenders.

statute_title: Shoplifting (Concealment of Merchandise)
offense_class: Depends on value — Petty Misdemeanor to Class B Felony
elements: Defendant concealed merchandise of a retail store
With intent to defraud the merchant
Without paying the purchase price
notes: Shoplifting is prosecuted under the general theft statute based on value of goods taken. Concealment of merchandise gives rise to inference of intent to steal.

statute_title: Burglary in the First Degree
offense_class: Class B Felony (first degree); Class C Felony (second degree, HRS § 708-811)
elements: Defendant intentionally entered or remained unlawfully in a building
With intent to commit therein a crime against a person or against property rights
First degree: was recklessly disregarding risk that building was occupied, OR was armed, OR caused physical injury
notes: First degree burglary requires either that building was occupied, defendant was armed, or injury was caused. Second degree is entry with criminal intent without aggravating factors.

statute_title: Burglary in the First Degree — Dwelling
elements: Defendant intentionally entered or remained unlawfully in a building
Building was a dwelling or the defendant recklessly disregarded the risk it was occupied
Defendant intended to commit a crime therein
enhancements: Occupant was present and suffered injury
notes: Entry into an occupied dwelling is automatically first degree burglary in Hawaii.

statute_title: Burglary in the Second Degree
elements: Defendant intentionally entered or remained unlawfully in a building
With intent to commit therein a crime against a person or property rights
No first-degree aggravating factors present
enhancements: Use of tools or instruments to gain entry
notes: Second degree covers non-dwelling burglary without aggravating factors such as occupancy, weapons, or injury.

statute_title: Unauthorized Control of Propelled Vehicle
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly exerted unauthorized control over another's propelled vehicle
By operating the vehicle without the owner's consent
enhancements: Use of vehicle in commission of another felony
Vehicle valued over $20,000 (may also be charged as first degree theft)
notes: UCPV is Hawaii's primary motor vehicle theft statute. Also known as joyriding. Can be charged alongside theft depending on intent.

statute_title: Theft — Receiving Stolen Property
elements: Defendant received, retained, or disposed of the property of another
Knowing that it had been stolen
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Prosecuted under Hawaii's consolidated theft statute. Degree determined by value of stolen property received.

statute_title: Criminal Property Damage in the First Degree
offense_class: Class B Felony (first, $20,000+); Class C Felony (second, $1,500+, HRS § 708-821); Misdemeanor (third, $500+, HRS § 708-822); Petty Misdemeanor (fourth, under $500, HRS § 708-823)
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly damaged the property of another
Without the owner's consent
Degree depends on value of damage or nature of property
enhancements: Damage to a utility or public infrastructure (first degree regardless of value)
notes: Hawaii uses criminal property damage rather than vandalism. Four degrees based on value of damage.

statute_title: Criminal Trespass in the Second Degree
offense_class: Petty Misdemeanor (second degree); Misdemeanor (first degree, HRS § 708-813)
elements: Defendant knowingly entered or remained unlawfully in or upon premises
Premises were enclosed in a manner designed to exclude intruders OR premises were fenced or property of the state
enhancements: First degree: commercial premises at night, dwelling, or with dangerous instrument
notes: First degree criminal trespass (HRS § 708-813) is a misdemeanor and applies to dwelling entries, commercial premises at night, or when carrying dangerous instruments.

statute_title: Criminal Property Damage (Criminal Mischief)
offense_class: Varies by degree — Class B Felony to Petty Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant intentionally damaged property of another
OR recklessly damaged property of another in the course of committing a crime
notes: Hawaii uses 'criminal property damage' as its equivalent of criminal mischief. Same statutes as vandalism entry.

statute_title: Abuse of Family or Household Members
offense_class: Misdemeanor (first offense); Class C Felony (with prior conviction within 2 years under HRS § 709-906(9))
penalty_max: 1 year (first offense misdemeanor); 5 years (felony for repeat)
elements: Defendant physically abused a family or household member
Family or household members include spouses, former spouses, persons in a dating relationship, persons with a common child, persons related by blood, and cohabitants
mandatory_minimum: 48 hours (first offense with prior conviction); 15 days (if prior TRO violation); 30 days (second TRO violation)
enhancements: Prior conviction within 2 years (Class C felony)
notes: Mandatory arrest required for domestic abuse calls. Court must order domestic violence intervention assessment. No-contact order imposed during pendency of the case.

statute_title: Abuse of Family or Household Members — Physical Harm
offense_class: Misdemeanor; Class C Felony (repeat within 2 years)
elements: Defendant physically abused a family or household member
Causing bodily injury
notes: Hawaii does not have a separate domestic battery statute — all domestic violence is prosecuted under HRS § 709-906. Bodily injury cases may also be charged as assault.

statute_title: Endangering the Welfare of a Minor in the First Degree
offense_class: Class C Felony (first degree); Misdemeanor (second degree, HRS § 709-904)
elements: Defendant, being a parent, guardian, or other person responsible for the welfare of a minor
Intentionally or knowingly allowed the minor to be placed in a situation of substantial risk of serious harm
notes: Second degree (HRS § 709-904) covers lesser endangerment where parent or guardian knowingly endangers the child's welfare.

statute_title: Promoting Child Abuse in the First Degree
offense_class: Class A Felony (first degree); Class B Felony (second degree, HRS § 707-751); Class C Felony (third degree, HRS § 707-752)
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused substantial bodily injury to a minor under 18 (first degree)
OR recklessly caused substantial bodily injury to a minor (second degree)
OR caused bodily injury to a minor (third degree)
enhancements: Use of an instrument or weapon
notes: Hawaii specifically designates child abuse as 'promoting child abuse' in three degrees. First degree involves intentionally causing substantial bodily injury to a child.

statute_title: Violation of an Order for Protection
elements: A protective order was issued against the defendant
Defendant knowingly or intentionally violated the order
Violation involved contact with, or proximity to, the protected person
mandatory_minimum: 48 hours (if prior DV conviction); 15 days (second TRO violation)
enhancements: Physical contact or assault during violation
Violation accompanied by another criminal offense
notes: Hawaii has both temporary restraining orders (TROs) and protective orders. Violation of either is a criminal offense. Mandatory minimum jail time increases with each subsequent violation.

statute_title: Stalking in the First Degree
offense_class: Class C Felony (first degree); Misdemeanor (second degree, HRS § 711-1106.4)
elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly engaged in a course of conduct directed at a specific person
That would cause a reasonable person to feel fear for their safety or to suffer emotional distress
First degree requires prior conviction for stalking or violation of a TRO
enhancements: Stalking in violation of a TRO
notes: First degree stalking requires a prior conviction for stalking or a prior violation of a TRO against the same victim.

statute_title: Harassment
elements: Defendant, with intent to harass, annoy, or alarm another person
Struck, shoved, kicked, or otherwise touched another in an offensive manner
OR insulted, taunted, or challenged in a manner likely to provoke an immediate violent response
OR repeatedly made communications anonymously or at inconvenient hours
enhancements: Harassment by stalking (elevated to stalking charge)
notes: Harassment is a petty misdemeanor. Often used as a lesser included offense for assault cases.

statute_title: Abuse of Family or Household Members — Elder; Elder Abuse
offense_class: Misdemeanor to Class C Felony (criminal); Civil remedies also available
elements: Defendant abused, neglected, or exploited a vulnerable elder
Victim was 62 years or older or a dependent adult
notes: Elder abuse can be charged under the domestic violence statute (HRS § 709-906) if the victim is a family member, or under separate elder abuse provisions. Financial exploitation of elders is separately prosecuted.

statute_title: Carrying or Use of Firearm in the Commission of a Separate Felony; Possession of a Firearm with an Altered Serial Number
offense_class: Class A Felony (firearm use during felony); Class B Felony (altered serial number)
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm with intent to facilitate a felony
OR possessed a firearm with an altered, removed, or obliterated serial number
mandatory_minimum: Mandatory minimum term of imprisonment when firearm used in felony
notes: Hawaii has strict firearms regulations. Separate permits required for acquisition, registration, and carry. See HRS Chapter 134 for comprehensive firearms regulation.

statute_title: Ownership or Possession Prohibited — Convicted Felons
offense_class: Class B Felony (firearm); Class C Felony (ammunition)
elements: Defendant had been convicted of a felony or certain enumerated misdemeanors
Defendant owned, possessed, or controlled a firearm or ammunition
notes: Also prohibits firearm possession by persons convicted of domestic violence misdemeanors, persons adjudicated mentally defective, fugitives, illegal drug users, and illegal aliens.

statute_title: Licenses to Carry — Carrying Without a License
offense_class: Class B Felony (place to keep loaded or unloaded firearm, HRS § 134-6(c)-(e)); Misdemeanor (various permit violations)
elements: Defendant carried a firearm in public
Without a valid license to carry
OR carried in a prohibited location
enhancements: Carrying in a prohibited area (schools, government buildings)
notes: Hawaii requires a license to carry a concealed firearm. Following the Bruen decision, Hawaii updated its permitting system. Places of worship, schools, bars, and government buildings remain prohibited.

statute_title: Unlawful Discharge of a Firearm
elements: Defendant discharged a firearm
In a manner that endangered persons or property
In a populated area or without lawful justification
notes: Reckless discharge of a firearm is a separate offense from assault with a dangerous weapon.

statute_title: Restriction on Possession, Sale, Gift, or Delivery of Electric Guns and Other Prohibited Weapons
offense_class: Misdemeanor (electric guns); Class C Felony (switchblades, butterfly knives, and other prohibited weapons)
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed, manufactured, sold, or transported a prohibited weapon
Prohibited weapons include switchblades, butterfly knives, metal knuckles, and other specified weapons
notes: Hawaii prohibits many categories of weapons beyond firearms, including switchblade knives, butterfly knives, and metal knuckles.

statute_title: Identity Theft in the First Degree
offense_class: Class A Felony (first degree, $20,000+); Class B Felony (second degree, $300+, HRS § 708-839.7); Class C Felony (third degree, HRS § 708-839.8)
elements: Defendant made or caused to be made a transmission of personal information of another
By any oral statement, written statement, or electronically
Without authorization and with intent to commit fraud, harm, or profit
enhancements: Amount of financial harm exceeds thresholds
notes: Hawaii has three degrees of identity theft based on the amount of financial harm or number of victims. Includes computer fraud and unauthorized access.

statute_title: Theft by Deception or Breach of Fiduciary Obligation
offense_class: Depends on value — same as theft degrees (Class B Felony to Petty Misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant obtained or exerted control over property entrusted to them
In a fiduciary capacity
Used or disposed of the property in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the trust or fiduciary obligation
With intent to deprive the owner
enhancements: Value of embezzled funds determines degree
notes: Embezzlement is prosecuted under Hawaii's consolidated theft statute. No separate embezzlement crime — it falls under theft by deception or breach of fiduciary obligation.

statute_title: Forgery in the First Degree
offense_class: Class B Felony (first degree); Class C Felony (second degree, HRS § 708-852); Misdemeanor (third degree, HRS § 708-853)
elements: Defendant, with intent to defraud, falsely made, completed, endorsed, or altered a written instrument
OR uttered a forged instrument knowing it to be forged
First degree: government-issued instrument (money, stamps, securities)
notes: Three degrees based on the type of document forged. First degree covers government-issued instruments. Third degree covers general written instruments.

statute_title: Issuing a Bad Check
elements: Defendant issued a check knowing it would not be honored by the drawee
Check was not paid upon presentation
notes: Presumption of knowledge if check is not paid within 30 days of notice of dishonor.

statute_title: Insurance Fraud
elements: Defendant knowingly presented a false or fraudulent claim for payment
To an insurance company or self-insured entity
With intent to defraud
notes: Hawaii insurance fraud includes false motor vehicle accident claims, medical billing fraud, and staged accidents.

statute_title: Fraudulent Use of a Credit Card
elements: Defendant used a credit card or credit card number belonging to another
Without authorization and with intent to defraud
To obtain goods, services, or anything of value
notes: Also covers use of forged, expired, or revoked credit cards. Part of Hawaii's broader fraud offense framework.

statute_title: Money Laundering
elements: Defendant conducted or attempted to conduct a financial transaction
Knowing that the property involved represents the proceeds of specified unlawful activity
With intent to promote the carrying on of specified unlawful activity
OR knowing the transaction was designed to conceal the nature, location, source, ownership, or control of the proceeds
notes: Hawaii's money laundering statute (Chapter 708A) closely follows the federal model.

statute_title: Theft by Deception
offense_class: Depends on value — Class B Felony ($20,000+) to Petty Misdemeanor (under $250)
elements: Defendant obtained property of another by creating or reinforcing a false impression
Including false impressions of law, value, intention, or other state of mind
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: General fraud in Hawaii is prosecuted as theft by deception under the consolidated theft statute. Degree based on value of property obtained.

statute_title: Sexual Assault in the First Degree
elements: Defendant knowingly subjected another person to an act of sexual penetration
By compulsion through strong compulsion or by force
OR victim was less than 14 years old
OR victim was mentally defective or mentally incapacitated
mandatory_minimum: Indeterminate sentence with minimum set by parole authority
enhancements: Prior sex offense convictions (mandatory extended sentence)
notes: Hawaii uses 'sexual assault' rather than 'rape.' Four degrees exist. First degree (Class A) involves penetration by force or with a victim under 14.

statute_title: Sexual Assault in the First Degree (Hawaii Equivalent of Rape)
elements: Defendant knowingly subjected another to an act of sexual penetration by compulsion
Compulsion means the use of physical force or a threat of imminent death, serious bodily injury, or kidnapping
mandatory_minimum: Indeterminate life sentence or extended sentence may apply for repeat offenders
notes: Hawaii does not use the term 'rape' in its criminal code. Sexual assault in the first degree (HRS § 707-730) is the functional equivalent. Covers penetration by force or against a victim under 14.

statute_title: Indecent Exposure
elements: Defendant intentionally exposed their genitals to another person
Under circumstances in which the defendant's conduct was likely to cause affront or alarm
notes: Classified as a petty misdemeanor. Repeat offenses may result in sex offender registration requirements.

statute_title: Prostitution
elements: Defendant engaged in or agreed to engage in sexual conduct with another person
For a fee or compensation
enhancements: Promoting prostitution (Class B or C felony under HRS § 712-1202 to 712-1204)
Solicitation of a minor (Class A felony)
notes: Simple prostitution and solicitation are petty misdemeanors. Promoting prostitution carries much more serious penalties.

statute_title: Sexual Assault in the Third Degree
elements: Defendant recklessly subjected another to sexual contact
By compulsion or by threat of forcible compulsion
OR the victim was less than 14 years old
notes: Sexual contact offenses (as opposed to penetration) are covered under third and fourth degree sexual assault.

statute_title: Violation of Privacy in the First Degree — Intimate Images
elements: Defendant intentionally disclosed an image of another identifiable person
Whose intimate parts are exposed or who is engaged in a sexual act
Without the depicted person's consent and with intent to harm
enhancements: Use of electronic media for wide distribution
notes: Hawaii's revenge porn and non-consensual intimate image distribution law. Also covers voyeurism under HRS § 711-1110.9.

statute_title: Promoting Child Abuse in the First, Second, and Third Degree; Electronic Enticement of a Child (HRS § 707-756)
offense_class: Class A Felony (promoting child abuse first); Class B Felony (electronic enticement); Class C Felony (promoting child abuse third)
penalty_max: 20 years (first degree promoting); 10 years (electronic enticement); 5 years (third degree promoting)
elements: Defendant produced, distributed, or possessed child sexual abuse material
OR used a computer or electronic device to entice a minor to engage in sexual conduct
notes: Electronic enticement of a child (HRS § 707-756) specifically targets online predatory behavior. Sex offender registration required upon conviction.

statute_title: Failure to Comply with Sex Offender Registration Requirements
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender under HRS Chapter 846E
Defendant knowingly failed to register, verify information, or update registration as required
notes: Sex offender registration in Hawaii is maintained by the Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center. Registration periods vary based on the tier of the offense.

statute_title: Sexual Assault in the First Degree — Victim Under 14
elements: Defendant knowingly subjected a person under 14 to an act of sexual penetration
Regardless of consent
mandatory_minimum: Extended term of imprisonment may be imposed
enhancements: Defendant in a position of authority
notes: Hawaii's age of consent is 16. Sexual penetration with a victim under 14 is first degree sexual assault (Class A felony). Third degree sexual assault (HRS § 707-732) covers contact offenses with victims under 14.

statute_title: Sexual Assault in the Fourth Degree
elements: Defendant knowingly subjected another person to sexual contact
Without the other person's consent or by compulsion
notes: Fourth degree sexual assault covers non-consensual sexual contact. Hawaii does not use the term 'sexual battery' — this is the functional equivalent.

statute_title: Disorderly Conduct
elements: Defendant, with intent to cause physical inconvenience or alarm
Engaged in fighting or violent behavior, made unreasonable noise, or created a hazardous condition
By an act which was not necessary for any lawful purpose
notes: Disorderly conduct is a petty misdemeanor. Common charge in cases involving public disturbances, loud parties, or fights.

statute_title: Resisting Arrest
elements: Defendant intentionally prevented a peace officer acting under color of official authority
From effecting an arrest
By using or threatening to use physical force against the peace officer or another
enhancements: Fleeing in a vehicle (separate charge under HRS § 710-1026.8/1026.9)
notes: The arrest does not need to be lawful for the charge to apply. Physical force or threat of force against the officer is required.

statute_title: Hindering Prosecution
offense_class: Class C Felony (hindering prosecution of felony); Misdemeanor (hindering prosecution of misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant rendered assistance to a person who had committed a crime
With intent to hinder the detection, apprehension, prosecution, conviction, or punishment of another
By harboring, concealing, warning, providing means of escape, suppressing evidence, or aiding flight
enhancements: The underlying offense was a felony (elevates to Class C felony)
notes: Also see tampering with a witness (HRS § 710-1071) and tampering with evidence (HRS § 710-1076).

statute_title: Criminal Contempt of Court
elements: Defendant intentionally or recklessly violated a court order or engaged in disruptive conduct in court
The order was lawful and the defendant had knowledge of it
notes: Criminal contempt is separate from civil contempt, which is used to compel compliance. Criminal contempt is punitive.

statute_title: Intoxication (Hawaii Approach)
offense_class: Not criminalized as a standalone offense
elements: Hawaii does not criminalize public intoxication as a standalone offense
notes: Hawaii does not have a public intoxication statute. Intoxicated individuals creating disturbances may be charged with disorderly conduct (HRS § 711-1101) or taken to a detoxification facility under HRS § 334-1.

statute_title: Loitering (Various County Ordinances)
elements: Defendant remained in a public place without apparent purpose
Under circumstances that warrant alarm for the safety of persons or property
notes: Loitering laws in Hawaii are primarily governed by county ordinances rather than state statute. Enforceability has been subject to constitutional challenges.

statute_title: Disorderly Conduct (Disturbing the Peace)
elements: Defendant made unreasonable noise or engaged in offensive conduct
With intent to cause public inconvenience, annoyance, or alarm
notes: Hawaii covers disturbing the peace under its disorderly conduct statute (HRS § 711-1101).

statute_title: Bail Jumping
offense_class: Class C Felony (if underlying charge is felony); Misdemeanor (if underlying charge is misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant was released on bail or recognizance
Defendant intentionally failed to appear in court as required
enhancements: Underlying charge was a serious felony
notes: Bail jumping in Hawaii is graded based on the seriousness of the underlying charge.

statute_title: False Reporting to Law Enforcement Authorities
elements: Defendant intentionally made a false report to law enforcement
That a crime had been committed
Knowing the report was false
enhancements: False report causes emergency response deployment
False report targets a specific individual (swatting)
notes: Also covers false reports regarding emergencies and furnishing false information to law enforcement.

statute_title: Terroristic Threatening in the First Degree
offense_class: Class C Felony (first degree); Misdemeanor (second degree, HRS § 707-717)
elements: Defendant threatened, by word or conduct, to cause bodily injury to another person
OR to cause damage to property of another
With the intent to terrorize or with reckless disregard that the threat would cause terror
First degree: threat to cause death, use of a dangerous instrument, or threat causes evacuation of a building
notes: Hawaii calls this 'terroristic threatening' rather than criminal threat. Two degrees based on severity.

statute_title: Revocation of Probation
offense_class: Court may revoke probation and impose original sentence
penalty_max: Original sentence for the underlying offense
elements: Defendant was placed on probation for a criminal offense
Defendant violated a term or condition of probation
Violation was inexcusable
enhancements: New criminal offense committed while on probation
notes: Court has discretion to modify conditions, extend probation, or revoke probation and impose the original sentence. Graduated sanctions may be imposed.

statute_title: Technical Violation of Probation
offense_class: Court discretion — modification to full revocation
elements: Defendant violated a technical condition of probation
Such as missed appointments, failed drug tests, or curfew violations
Without committing a new criminal offense
notes: Courts may use graduated sanctions for technical violations before revoking probation. Hawaii uses a progressive discipline model.

statute_title: Substantive Violation of Probation — New Criminal Offense
offense_class: Court may revoke probation and impose original sentence; new offense charged separately
penalty_max: Original sentence plus sentence for new offense
elements: Defendant was on probation and committed a new criminal offense
notes: A new criminal offense while on probation typically results in revocation. The new offense is charged separately and may result in consecutive sentences.

statute_title: Parole Revocation
offense_class: Administrative/judicial — return to imprisonment for remainder of term
elements: Defendant was released on parole
Defendant violated a condition of parole
enhancements: New criminal offense while on parole
notes: Hawaii Paroling Authority sets parole conditions and determines violations. Revocation returns the parolee to serve the remainder of the original sentence.

statute_title: Criminal Conspiracy
offense_class: Same class as the target offense (reduced by one level for Class A felonies)
penalty_max: Same as target offense (20 years max for Class A)
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to engage in or cause conduct constituting a crime
With intent to promote or facilitate the commission of the crime
An overt act in pursuance of the conspiracy was committed by defendant or co-conspirator
notes: Conspiracy is graded at the same level as the target offense. An overt act is required. Renunciation is an affirmative defense.

statute_title: Use of Force in Self-Protection
offense_class: Affirmative defense — not a criminal charge
elements: Defendant believed force was immediately necessary to protect against the use of unlawful force by another
Force used was proportional to the threat
Deadly force may be used only when the defendant believed it was necessary to protect against death, serious bodily injury, kidnapping, or sexual assault
notes: Hawaii imposes a duty to retreat if safely possible before using deadly force. No 'Stand Your Ground' law. Castle Doctrine applies within the home (HRS § 703-304(5)(b)).

statute_title: Miscellaneous Hawaii Criminal Offenses
elements: Elements specific to each offense as defined under the Hawaii Revised Statutes
notes: Catch-all for Hawaii offenses not otherwise enumerated. Consult the specific HRS section for elements, penalties, and defenses.
